clue.text: Horror-struck scallywag has turned to bottle

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so the letters are read backwards
to bottle something is to hold it inside, so the answer sits held within the run of words

parts.note: the run of letters across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A rascal is so frightened that he has lost his nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: Read wAG HAS T from right to left and AGHAST appears. 'Turned' does double duty: it gives the final letter of the run and also signals the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone filled with sudden shock and dread at something terrible.

clue.text: Thought one would snarl about contemptible supporter?

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps itself around the other

parts.note: felt is a past tense of think, as in 'I felt it was wrong'
low behaviour is base and despicable
to snarl a thread is to tangle or ravel it, so one who does so is a raveller

explanation.surface: Someone assumed a person would growl at a despised hanger-on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snarl' suggests growling, but here it means tangle; 'contemptible supporter' looks like one phrase, yet the first word goes inside the past tense and the definition is the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a sympathiser of a political movement, especially Communism, who backs its aims without joining as a party member.

clue.text: Believers in AA run it out, initially sceptical

indicators.note: letters put out of their places are disordered and must be rearranged
initially means at the beginning, so only the opening letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: Members of Alcoholics Anonymous who are believers run the meeting, the doubters at first excluded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link word joining definition to wordplay, but it belongs to the letters being rearranged; without it the count falls two short.
explanation.definitionFit: Unitarians are a Christian denomination who reject the Trinity, so they are a body of believers.

clue.text: Protected church — provide walls

indicators.note: to wall something is to surround it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: to fend for someone is to provide for them
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A church that is protected because someone paid for its walls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'walls' reads as a noun about the church building, but it is a verb meaning surrounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A fenced area is enclosed by a barrier, which keeps it safe and guarded from intruders.

clue.text: Badly need job — one installed as Democrat

indicators.note: a thing installed is fitted inside something else, so one piece goes within
something done badly is botched, so the letters come out in a muddled order

explanation.surface: A desperate job-seeker is appointed as a Democratic Party candidate.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters are split so that the single-letter numeral sits inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe Biden is a member of the US Democratic Party who served as its president, so he is an example of one.

clue.text: Amazonian people in one place to the north

indicators.note: in a down entry, going north means travelling upwards, so the letters run bottom to top

parts.note: to place something is to put it

explanation.surface: A tribe from the Amazon is found living in a single northern spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to the north' seems to locate the place geographically, but in a down clue it tells the solver to read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tupi are an indigenous group of Brazil living in the Amazon basin and along the coast.

clue.text: First from Christopher Marlowe, living deceptively: English dramatist

indicators.note: something presented deceptively is disguised, so the letters are rearranged to mislead
taking the first from a word means keeping just its opening letter

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An English playwright follows the lead of Christopher Marlowe, who lived a life of deception and espionage.
explanation.walkthrough: Marlowe looks like the answer's subject, but his name is only raw letters. 'English' reads as describing the dramatist, yet it also supplies a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Congreve was a Restoration playwright, author of The Way of the World, so he is an example of a writer of plays.

clue.text: Answer found in song to lift a curse

indicators.note: a thing found in another is located inside it, so one piece is placed within

parts.note: an anthem is a rousing song meant to raise the spirits
A is the usual abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: Singing a particular song is the solution to break a spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to lift a curse' reads as one phrase about breaking a spell, but 'to lift' describes the song and the definition is the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Anathema originally meant a formal church ban or excommunication, and more broadly a solemn imprecation of damnation.

clue.text: Volunteer involved with region in Persian protests

indicators.note: involved means tangled together, so the letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A volunteer from one part of Iran joins street demonstrations.
explanation.walkthrough: The Green Movement was the wave of Iranian protests after the disputed 2009 election, named for the green of opposition candidate Mousavi's campaign.
explanation.definitionFit: The name was given by Western media to the 2009 Iranian demonstrations, and Iran was historically called Persia.

clue.text: Vote to exclude leader's share

indicators.note: excluding the leader means leaving off whatever comes at the front

explanation.surface: A proposal to vote a party leader out of their portion of power.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition rather than marking possession.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot is to distribute or apportion something among people, giving each a portion.

clue.text: Accountant with vivacity allowed in carriage

explanation.surface: A lively accountant is permitted to ride in a coach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'allowed in' reads like an insertion instruction, but nothing goes inside anything; 'in' simply joins the parts to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabriolet is a light two-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle with a folding hood, the source of the word cab.

clue.text: Thorn at the start to be in red, red rose

indicators.note: at the start points to the very beginning of the word, its opening letter

parts.note: to be in the red is to be in debt, which is to owe

explanation.surface: A gardener's note about a thorny red rose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rose' looks like the flower, but it is the past tense of rise, the verb the answer matches.
explanation.definitionFit: Towered means rose high or stood tall above surroundings, the past tense matching the verb sense of rose.

clue.text: State emphatically cleared out disreputable Irish county

indicators.note: a word with its contents cleared out keeps only its two outermost letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
County Clare is on the west coast of Ireland

explanation.surface: Someone insists that a rough part of Ireland has been cleaned up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cleared out' looks like a verb about the county, but it acts on the next word, emptying it of its middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To declare is to announce something firmly and openly, asserting it with conviction.

clue.text: Mad comic panel doing what's expected

indicators.note: mad means crazed and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A wild comic strip panel behaves exactly as you would predict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comic panel' reads as a frame from a cartoon strip, but the two words are only raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Compliance is acting in accordance with rules, requests or orders, behaving as one is required to.

clue.text: Legally land aquatic reptile losing leg

indicators.note: something losing a part has that part taken away from it

parts.note: a terrapin is a freshwater turtle

explanation.surface: A turtle that has lost a limb comes ashore lawfully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legally' looks like an adverb for the landing, but it qualifies the definition: the answer is the Latin word for land used in legal phrases.
explanation.definitionFit: Terra is Latin for earth or ground and appears in legal terms such as terra nullius.

clue.text: Leaves box and coaches close to street

parts.note: to coach someone is to teach them

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is used

explanation.surface: Someone departs from a boxing match as coaches near the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' and 'box' look like verbs, but together they define a container for tea leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea chest is a large wooden crate originally used to ship tea leaves, so it is a box for leaves.

clue.text: Have some tomorrow night

indicators.note: some means a portion, so only part of the following words is used

parts.note: the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: An invitation to enjoy a little something tomorrow evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have some' sounds like an offer of food or drink, but 'Have' is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To own something is to possess it, which is one sense of have.

clue.text: Reactionaries one used to give protection on train?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the conservative members of a group resisting change

definitions.text: one used to give protection on train?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: read literally, a former railway official who looked after a train

explanation.surface: Conservatives were once employed as security on the railways.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful literal reading: a guard who used to work on trains is an old guard. On British trains the guard is the conductor.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names long-standing members of a group who resist reform, from Napoleon's veteran Imperial Guard.

clue.text: Scornful sort called out for coffee

indicators.note: something called out is spoken, so it is the sound of the words that counts

parts.note: a mocker is one who scoffs; in a non-rhotic British accent the two words sound alike

explanation.surface: A sneering customer shouts out an order for a coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: The match relies on a British accent in which the final r of the scoffer's word is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocha is a fine coffee originally shipped from the Yemeni port of that name, now also a chocolate-flavoured drink.

clue.text: Warned a recording contains issues regularly avoided

indicators.note: to contain is to hold inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a DVD is a disc recording

indicators.note: avoiding at regular intervals means skipping every second letter and keeping the rest

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: Someone was cautioned that a recording touches on topics people tend to steer clear of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'issues regularly avoided' reads as subjects people shun, but it tells the solver to drop alternate letters of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To advise someone of a danger is to inform or caution them about it, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Confusion as base guards left gate unoccupied

indicators.note: a guard stands around what it protects, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: base and mean both describe low, ignoble behaviour
L is the abbreviation for left

indicators.note: an unoccupied word has had its inside emptied, keeping only the outer letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Chaos at a military base where the sentries abandoned the gate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'base' suggests a military camp, but it is an adjective meaning low or ignoble.
explanation.definitionFit: A melange is a mixture or jumble of different elements, a muddle in the sense of confusion.

clue.text: Man first to recover without heroin: he used to score

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece sits round the other
the first to a word is its opening letter, which alone is kept

explanation.surface: An addict recovering without heroin used to score drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without heroin' sounds like going clean, but it means the man goes around the drug. 'Score' is not buying drugs but writing music.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Mahler was an Austrian composer, and to score is to write orchestral music, so he is a former scorer.

clue.text: Puff away: not fit any more?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: blow air out of the lungs
second meaning: read as two parts, formerly healthy, since ex means former and hale means fit

explanation.surface: A smoker puffing on cigarettes wonders whether they have lost their fitness.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the split reading of the word as a former state of health.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhale is to breathe out, sending a puff of air away from the body.

clue.text: Stop woman receiving fine for misleading statement

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: F is the pencil-grading abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: An order to stop a woman who is paying a penalty for lying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fine' looks like a penalty, but it is the single-letter abbreviation, and it lands inside the first word rather than inside the woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A half-truth tells only part of the story so as to deceive, which makes it misleading without being an outright lie.

clue.text: Flab-tightening procedure for corpulent friar

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a cosmetic operation such as a tummy job
second meaning: the stout jolly friar of the Robin Hood legends

explanation.surface: A tummy operation for an overweight monk.
explanation.walkthrough: Friar Tuck is the plump, merry member of Robin Hood's band in English folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuck names both a surgical tightening of loose skin and the famously round friar of legend.

clue.text: The girl alas in retreat releasing the odd cry

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the letters are read from the end
releasing the odd ones lets every first, third and fifth go, keeping only the even-placed letters

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A girl backing away with a sigh lets out a strange cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the odd' looks like an adjective for the cry, but it means the odd-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Aargh is an exclamation of frustration, pain or horror, so it is an inarticulate shout.

clue.text: Spar with clever dicky over money for PM

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for shaky or faulty, so the letters are unsound and rearranged

parts.note: pence are British coins, and so money

explanation.surface: Arguing with a sharp operator with a weak heart over the Prime Minister's cash.
explanation.walkthrough: Spencer Perceval was the British Prime Minister shot dead in the House of Commons lobby in 1812, the only one ever assassinated.
explanation.definitionFit: Perceval held office as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1809 until his murder in 1812.
